main.t: The J-shaped bag between the oesophagus and the duodenum that holds food, churns it and starts digesting protein.
main.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The stomach’s J shape.

simpler.t: Your stomach stores a meal and mixes it with acid juices before passing it on.

deeper.t: It turns food into chyme and releases it into the small intestine a little at a time.

facts.t: It lies just below the oesophagus and links it to the duodenum.
Its two ends are fixed; the part between them can move and change size.

simpler.t: It sits in the upper abdomen, under the diaphragm, mostly on the left.
simpler.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). That the stomach lies mostly on the left.

deeper.t: The lesser omentum ties it to the liver; the greater omentum hangs from its greater curvature.

items.name: Cardia
items.t: Where the oesophagus joins and food enters.

items.name: Fundus
items.t: The dome above and to the left of the cardia, under the diaphragm.

items.name: Body
items.t: The main part of the stomach.

items.name: Pylorus
items.t: The funnel to the duodenum, ending at the pyloric sphincter, which controls emptying.

items.name: Rugae
items.t: Large folds of mucosa and submucosa that form when the stomach is empty.

simpler.t: Four regions, from top to bottom: cardia, fundus, body and pylorus.

deeper.t: It has an extra, inner oblique layer of smooth muscle, so it can churn food vigorously.

facts.t: Empty it is about the size of a fist, yet it can stretch to hold about 4 litres.
Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor; chief cells make pepsinogen.
Mucus rich in bicarbonate, tight junctions and fast cell renewal protect the stomach from digesting itself.

simpler.t: It stretches to hold a meal, makes strong acid, and protects itself with a mucus lining.

items.name: Oesophagus
items.t: Enters through the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm and joins at the cardia.

items.name: Duodenum
items.t: Receives chyme through the pyloric sphincter.

items.name: Liver
items.t: Joined to the lesser curvature by the lesser omentum.

items.name: Greater omentum
items.t: Runs from the greater curvature to the posterior abdominal wall.

items.name: Gastrin
items.t: Made mainly by G cells of the pyloric antrum. It increases gastric secretion and emptying.

simpler.t: Food comes in from the oesophagus and goes on to the duodenum.

facts.t: It develops as a widening of the foregut, the same tube that also gives rise to the lung bud.
facts.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The development of the stomach from the foregut.

facts.t: Its size and position change with every meal, as it fills, churns and empties.

items.injury: Long use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as aspirin, or Helicobacter pylori infection.
items.damaged: The mucosal barrier, letting acid erode the lining (a peptic ulcer).
items.why: Gastric juice eats deeper into the unprotected mucosa.

items.injury: An ulcer that erodes right through the stomach wall.
items.damaged: The whole wall, now perforated, and the peritoneum.
items.why: Stomach contents leak through the hole and inflame the peritoneum (peritonitis).

items.q: Explain why the stomach does not digest itself.
model: A thick mucus coat rich in bicarbonate neutralises acid.
Tight junctions stop gastric juice getting between the cells.
Stem cells replace damaged surface cells quickly.
Together these form the mucosal barrier.

items.q: Compare parietal cells and chief cells.
model: Both lie in the gastric glands.
Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
The acid converts pepsinogen into active pepsin.

items.q: Predict the effect of the enterogastric reflex when the duodenum fills with chyme.
model: Distension of the duodenum triggers the reflex.
So no more chyme enters until the duodenum is ready.

check.why: Parietal cells produce hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.

check.stem: Which region of the stomach connects to the duodenum?
check.why: The funnel-shaped pylorus connects the stomach to the duodenum.
The majority of ulcers are caused by NSAIDs or Helicobacter pylori infection.
